title: Designing a CI Pipeline
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of designing a ci pipeline and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to designing a ci pipeline.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on designing a ci pipeline. A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Designing a CI Pipeline matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Defining pipeline objectives
items.text: For defining pipeline objectives, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Pipeline stages and dependencies
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Fast checks versus comprehensive checks
items.text: For fast checks versus comprehensive checks, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Choosing workflow triggers
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Establishing a clear pass/fail outcome
items.text: For establishing a clear pass/fail outcome, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Pull request CI
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run tests
        run: echo "Replace with the project test command"
content_blocks.expected_output: Pushes and pull requests trigger a read-only validation job; replace the demonstration command with the project test suite.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a disposable branch and verify that failed tests cause a failed status check.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Configure required checks to match the actual workflow and test command.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to designing a ci pipeline. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain designing a ci pipeline, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.task: Apply designing a ci pipeline to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: A CI pipeline should run relevant fast checks, tests, and build steps on change events and produce clear, required pass/fail checks.

A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
